purpose: Thiothixene is used to treat schizophrenia and other conditions where a person experiences symptoms like hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized thinking. It helps reduce these symptoms so you can think more clearly and function better in daily life. Your doctor may also use it for other mental health conditions as they see fit.
how_it_works: Your brain uses chemical messengers called neurotransmitters to send signals. In schizophrenia, a chemical called dopamine can become overactive in certain areas of the brain. Thiothixene works by blocking dopamine receptors, which helps calm down those overactive signals and reduces symptoms like hearing voices or having unusual beliefs.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or feeling sleepy, dizziness especially when standing up quickly, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and weight changes. Some people may notice restlessness, muscle stiffness, or involuntary muscle movements – let your doctor know right away if this happens.
warnings: This medication can cause a serious condition called tardive dyskinesia – uncontrolled repetitive movements of the face or body – which may be permanent. It can also lower your blood pressure when you stand up, so rise slowly. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication. Elderly patients with dementia who take antipsychotics have a higher risk of stroke or death. Do not stop taking this medication suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: For most adults, the starting dose is usually 2 mg taken 2 to 3 times a day by mouth. Your doctor may slowly increase this based on how you respond, often up to 20–30 mg per day in divided doses. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never adjust your dose on your own.
